(a) Let N_s be the number of lattice sites along each direction and a = L_phy/N_s the lattice spacing. With periodic boundary conditions, allowed momenta are k_i = 2πm_i/L_phy, restricted to the first Brillouin zone. For flavor f = n,p and spin s = ↑,↓, define

a†_{kfs} = N_s^(−3/2) Σ_r exp(i k·r) a†_{rfs},     |k,f,s⟩ = a†_{kfs}|0⟩.

These momentum states form a single-particle basis. For total momentum P, a spin-singlet pair, for distinct one-particle modes, is

|k,P−k;f,g;S=0⟩ = (a†_{kf↑}a†_{P−k,g↓} − a†_{kf↓}a†_{P−k,g↑})|0⟩/√2.

At P = 0, the neutron-neutron, proton-proton, and neutron-proton examples are

|nn;k⟩ = (n†_{k↑}n†_{−k↓} − n†_{k↓}n†_{−k↑})|0⟩/√2,
|pp;k⟩ = (p†_{k↑}p†_{−k↓} − p†_{k↓}p†_{−k↑})|0⟩/√2,
|np;k⟩ = (n†_{k↑}p†_{−k↓} − n†_{k↓}p†_{−k↑})|0⟩/√2.

For identical particles (nn or pp), a spin singlet has an even relative spatial wavefunction. The k and −k descriptions must therefore be counted consistently, without double counting. At k = 0 the displayed identical-particle expression is not normalized as written; for example, the normalized nn state is n†_{0↑}n†_{0↓}|0⟩. The interaction displayed in the question acts on components 1 and 2 (typically n↑ and n↓); equal interactions in other flavor channels would be an additional assumption.

(b) Fourier transformation of the free lattice Hamiltonian gives

ε_lat(k) = 2t Σ_{i=1}^3 [1 − cos(k_i a)].

The literal lowest periodic-box mode is k = 0 and has zero kinetic energy in both descriptions, so matching that mode cannot determine t. Interpreting the requested matching as applying to the lowest nonzero mode, take k = (2π/L_phy, 0, 0). Its lattice energy is 2t[1 − cos(2π/N_s)], while its continuum energy is (2π/L_phy)^2/(2M_phy). Equating them gives the exact finite-lattice result

t = π² / {M_phy L_phy²[1 − cos(2π/N_s)]}.

For large N_s, 1 − cos(2π/N_s) ≈ 2π²/N_s². Since a = L_phy/N_s, this yields the continuum-limit behavior t → 1/(2M_phy a²).

(c) The matched lowest nonzero single-particle energy is

E_min = (2πℏc/L_phy)²/(2M_phy).

Using ℏc = 197.326 MeV·fm, L_phy = 3.4 fm, and M_phy = 1634 MeV gives E_min ≈ 40.7 MeV. This is the lowest nonzero momentum energy; the k = 0 mode still has zero kinetic energy.

(d) Write U = Ct for the on-site interaction in the specified channel, and consider a pair of total momentum zero. Its relative two-particle kinetic energy at momentum k is 2ε_lat(k). For a contact interaction, the momentum-space interaction matrix element is constant. The bound-state equation at E = −B therefore gives

1 = −U (1/N_s³) Σ_k 1/[B + 2ε_lat(k)],     B = 17.8 MeV.

Thus, for a specified lattice spacing and cutoff,

C = −{t (1/N_s³) Σ_k 1/[B + 2ε_lat(k)]}^(−1).

In the thermodynamic limit at fixed lattice spacing, let q = ka and replace the normalized sum by an integral over the Brillouin zone. Since 2ε_lat = 4t Σ_i[1 − cos(q_i)],

C = −1/J(B/t),
J(x) = ∫_[−π,π]³ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[x + 4Σ_i(1 − cos(q_i))].

This is a regulated relation, not a unique numerical value for C from B alone: evaluating it requires the lattice spacing (or equivalently the ultraviolet cutoff) and the corresponding t. The thermodynamic limit L → ∞ at fixed a is not the same as the continuum limit a → 0. In the latter, a three-dimensional zero-range interaction still requires cutoff-dependent renormalization. For example, with a sharp relative-momentum cutoff Λ, a continuum contact strength g obeys

1/g = −M_phy/(2π²)[Λ − κ arctan(Λ/κ)],     κ = √(M_phy B).

The binding energy fixes a physical scale but not the bare lattice coupling without a regulator prescription. In the standard zero-range s-wave interpretation, κ ≈ 170.5 MeV and the scattering length is a_s = ℏc/κ ≈ 1.16 fm.

At fixed total momentum P = 0, the bound state is at −17.8 MeV and the unbound relative-motion spectrum is continuous, E = k²/M_phy ≥ 0. The threshold is therefore 0 MeV; it is not a discrete, normalizable first-excited state.

(e) In the stated infinite-volume limit there is no discrete second-excited energy or finite level degeneracy to calculate. Above the bound state the spectrum is a continuum of scattering states, not a sequence of box levels. A discrete second level and its degeneracy would require a finite-volume spectrum and a specified lattice spacing or other regulator. Thus the numerical bare C and discrete excited-state energies are underdetermined as stated; the regulated relation and continuum threshold above are what can be specified without those additional inputs.
